editorial_contributions.text: The article under review is devoted to the investigation and summarizing of various results concerning the so-called \textit{unit theorem} that is a theorem from algebra which has a combinatoric flavor and that originated, in fact, from algebraic combinatorics. Specifically, the unit theorem claims that if \(F\) is a field and \(A\) a finite-dimensional algebra over \(F\) having an additive subgroup \(H\) that spans \(A\) as an \(F\)-vector space, then \(H\) contains a unit of \(A\). Beyond his ingenious proof given in the paper, the author also addresses some interesting applications, one of which is a proof of the well-known normal basis theorem from Galois theory. The paper is written in a fascinating style and also contains too many exercises in order to make up the work more nearly self-contained and friendly to the interested readers.

In this article H. W. Lenstra, jun., one of the discoverers of the most famous algorithm for lattices, the so-called LLL algorithm for lattice basis reduction, gives an excellent survey on lattices and their predominant role for important applications in number theory and other areas. In the first few sections he introduces lattices and some of their properties. Presentations of lattices are either via a basis or by a Gram matrix. Then he discusses the problem of finding shortest vectors. This is followed by applications to Diophantine approximations and to the nearest vector problem. Lattices of rank 2 are treated as a special case. In the following 2 sections Lenstra presents his concept of flags which boils down to constructing lattices \(L\) of dimension \(n\) as sequences of suitable sublattices \(L_1,\dots,L_n\) of dimension \(\dim(L_i)=i\). The last 4 sections are on important applications of lattice methods: factoring polynomials, linear algebra over rings, some nonlinear problems, and lattices over polynomial rings.

editorial_contributions.text:
This paper consists of a concise account of the history and solution of the misnamed Pell equation \(x^2 - D y^2 = 1,\) from its early history to modern techniques. Much of the discussion of early methods is centered around the ``cattle problem'' of Archimedes, including an English translation of the problem itself, a description (due to Amthor) of the problem's solution by way of solving an instance of Pell's equation, and a compact (only \(1/3\) of a page!) presentation of all solutions. Modern techniques for solving Pell's equation include the infrastructure methods (for both solving and representing the solutions themselves), and the state-of-the-art index-calculus algorithm. Hallgren's algorithm, that uses infrastructure to find solutions in polynomial time on a quantum computer, is also mentioned. The paper is self-contained, requiring only basic algebra, and includes detailed examples of important techniques. In short, this is an excellent source for a quick overview of modern methods and historical motivation surrounding this fascinating equation.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: A \textit{CM-order} is a reduced order equipped with an involution that mimics complex conjugation. The \textit{Witt-Picard group} of such an order is a certain group of ideal classes that is closely related to the ``minus part'' of the class group. We present a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for the following problem, which may be viewed as a special case of the principal ideal testing problem: given a CM-order, decide whether two given elements of its Witt-Picard group are equal. In order to prevent coefficient blow-up, the algorithm operates with lattices rather than with ideals. An important ingredient is a technique introduced by Gentry and Szydlo in a cryptographic context. Our application of it to lattices over CM-orders hinges upon a novel existence theorem for auxiliary ideals, which we deduce from a result of Konyagin and Pomerance in elementary number theory.

editorial_contributions.text: Cohen-Lenstra-Martinet (C-L-M for short) made some heuristics about the class groups of algebraic number fields given ``at random''. In the paper under review, the authors disprove the predictions of C-L-M in two different ways. On the one hand, they show that the heuristics of C-L-M are based on some facts which contradict some consequences of the Iwasawa Main Conjecture proved by \textit{B. Mazur} and \textit{A. Wiles} [Invent. Math. 76, 179--330 (1984; Zbl 0545.12005)]. On the other hand, they mention that the enumeration of algebraic number fields by discriminants may induce discrete probability distribution subfields. The authors formulate some heuristics in terms of Arakelov class groups of number fields. According to them, their formulation is confirming to the expectation that a mathematical object is isomorphic to a given object A with a probability inversely proportional to \#(Aut(A)). They also offer two formulations of C-L-M heuristics which they claim to be appropriate. The paper is rather technical and the results are obtained by using clever arguments.

editorial_contributions.text:
The integers are indeed a reality in our world, where many of their fascinating properties are mathematically easy to state, although not necessarily easy to prove. And modern algebra, even at the introductory level of groups, rings, and fields, can sometimes gratify us with an elegant, as though heavenly view to understanding why some of these arithmetic theorems hold. Here to illustrate, we look at the application of algebra in testing the primality of numbers of the form \(2^m\pm 1\), i.e., respectively, Pepin test for Fermat primes and Lucas-Lehmer test for Mersenne. As for computational implementation, either test would run through \(m\) recursive operations, mainly modular squaring.

Assuming proper attribution, one could use these notes as a suitable material for an extra lecture in a standard undergraduate abstract algebra class, especially that we are left with a small selection of very inviting exercises related to the two integer classes and the algebraic facts encountered along the way.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1582.11003].

editorial_contributions.text:
This paper gives a factorization method, which uses the multiplicative groups of elliptic curves over finite fields. The factorization method is probabilistic, with a conjectured expected running time for the factorization of n to be at most \((\log n)^ 2 \exp ((1+o(1))\sqrt{\log n\quad \log \log n}),\) for \(n\to \infty\). If the smallest prime factor of n is much smaller than \(\sqrt{n}\), the running time is expected to be shorter. 


The elliptic curve factoring method is inspired by Pollard's (p-1) factoring method. Instead of using the multiplicative group ( \({\mathbb{Z}}/n{\mathbb{Z}})^*\) in the Pollard method, the multiplicative group of an elliptic curve over \({\mathbb{Z}}/n{\mathbb{Z}}\) is used. Since the author does not want (and does not need) to go into the details of elliptic curves over finite rings he treats only elliptic curves over finite fields. In fact he only needs results for fields with a prime number of elements. Let \({\mathbb{F}}_ p\) be the finite field with p elements. The paper gives facts about the number of elliptic curves, over \({\mathbb{F}}_ p\), whose number of points is in a given subset of \({\mathbb{N}}\). Moreover he computes how many numbers in a given interval of \({\mathbb{N}}\) are completely composed of small prime factors. These results are combined to compute the expected run time of the algorithm. Unfortunately in this computation an unproven conjecture from analytic number theory was needed. However, it seems that the conjecture is true. 


At the end of the paper a comparison is made between the elliptic curve method and other factoring methods. One of the advantages of the elliptic curve method is that the storage requirements are much less than those for other methods of the same expected run time. It appears that the elliptic curve method is the fastest factorization method, with an exception for the quadratic sieve, for numbers composed of two prime numbers of about the same size. In addition, it seems favorable to use the elliptic curve method as a subroutine for other factoring methods.

editorial_contributions.text:
If \(X,Y\) are objects in a category \(\mathcal C\), then a correspondence from \(X\) to \(Y\) in \(\mathcal C\) is a triple \(c=(W,f,g)\), where \(W\) is an object of \(\mathcal C\) and \(f:W\to X\) and \(g:W\to Y\) are morphisms in \(\mathcal C\). A group commensurability, denoted \(c:X\leftrightharpoons Y\), is a correspondence \(c=(W,f,g)\) in the category of groups for which both \(f\) and \(g\) are isogenies, i.e., they are such that \(\#\ker f\), \(\#\ker g\), \((X:fW)\) and \((Y:gW)\) are finite. Then one defines \(i(f)=(X:fW)/\#\ker f\), \(i(g)=(Y:gW)/\#\ker g\) and \(i(c)=i(g)/i(f)\).

Let now \(Z\) be an infinite domain such that for all non-zero \(m\in Z\) the ring \(Z/mZ\) is finite, let \(Q\) be the field of fractions of \(Z\), let \(A\) be a semisimple \(Q\)-algebra of finite vector space dimension over \(Q\), let \(R\subset A\) be a sub-\(Z\)-algebra with \(Q\cdot R=A\) and let \(L\), \(M\) be finitely generated \(R\)-modules. In the main result of the paper, the authors prove that there is an \(R\)-module commensurability \(c:L\leftrightharpoons M\) if and only if the \(A\)-modules \(Q\otimes_Z L\) and \(Q\otimes_Z M\) are isomorphic. Moreover, whenever this is the case, they associate to \(c\) a ring commensurability \(e(c):\mathrm{End}L\leftrightharpoons \mathrm{End}M\) and a group commensurability \(a(c):\mathrm{Aut}L\leftrightharpoons \mathrm{Aut}M\) such that the indeces \(i(e(c))\) and \(i(a(c))\) do not depend on the particular choice of the commensurability \(c:L\leftrightharpoons M\). With this in mind, it is possible to define \(ia(L,M)=i(a(c))\). Furthermore, if both \(\#\mathrm{Aut}L\) and \(\#\mathrm{Aut}M\) are finite, it can be shown that \(ia(L,M)=\#\mathrm{Aut}M/\#\mathrm{Aut}L\), so that \(ia(L,M)\) can be seen as a generalization of the ratio of the size of the two automorphism groups to the case in which they have infinite orders. Some more properties of \(ia(L,M)\) are listed in Theorem 1.1.

The main motivation for developing the above theory comes from number theoretic implications related to the Cohen-Lenstra heuristics, which the authors want to address more in detail in a forthcoming paper. The idea is that when a mathematical object is drawn in some random manner, the probability that it is isomorphic to a given object is inversely proportional to the size of the automorphism group of the latter. The relevant objects in the application the authors have in mind are Arakelov class groups, which actually may have infinitely many automorphisms.

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \({\mathbb F}_5\) be the finite field with \(5\) elements, \(S\) the set of pairs \((f,g)\), \(f\in{\mathbb F}_5[X], \deg f=3\), \(g\in{\mathbb F}_5[X], \deg g=2\) such that \(f\cdot g=u\cdot\prod_{x\in {\mathbb F}_5}(X-x)\) for some \(u\in {\mathbb F}_5\setminus\{0\}\), \(T\) the set of irreducible polynomials in \({\mathbb F}_5[X]\) of degree \(3\). The author proves that the map 
\[
S\to t,(f,g)\mapsto f+g
\]
 is a bijection. He presents an algorithm that, given \(h\in T\), finds \((f,g)\in S\) with \(f+g=h\).

editorial_contributions.text: The number 43 is the smallest not mentioned positive integer in the first edition of [The Penguin dictionary of curious and interesting numbers. New York, NY: Penguin Books (1986)] by \textit{D. G. Wells}. In this enjoyable article the author demonstrates very convincingly how unjustified this is. Various observations he makes are consequences of the fact that 43 is an element in the Sylvester sequence defined by \(E_0=1\) and \(E_n=1+\prod_{t<n}E_t\) for \(n\geq 1\). The observation that \(2^{43}\equiv 3^{43}(\text{mod~}431)\) leads to some considerations related to Artin's primitive root conjecture. Various further interesting properties of 43 are given.

editorial_contributions.text:
The author considers the most important basic problems of algorithmic algebraic number theory: the determination of Galois groups, of the ring of integers, and of unit and class groups of algebraic number fields. He is exclusively interested in the complexity of the algorithms. Roughly speaking a ``good'' algorithm solves a problem in a running time which is polynomial in the length of the input data.


In a preliminary section it is shown that there are good algorithms for elementary arithmetic and basic tasks (linear algebra, basis reduction) in usually considered structures like finite fields (rings) and algebraic number fields. Whether the Galois group \(G\) of a non-zero polynomial over an algebraic number field \(K\) can be computed in polynomial time, is an open problem. This is mainly for the reason that we do not know of short representations of potential groups (as subgroups of \(S_ n\) for example) in general. At present the only affirmative answer can be given for abelian Galois groups and in case \(G\) is the symmetric or alternating group.


For the ring of integers \(O_ K\) of algebraic number fields \(K\) there is a negative result by Chistov saying that the determination of \(O_ K\) is polynomial time equivalent to the finding of the largest square factor of a given positive integer; and there are no good algorithms for solving that latter problem. The author shows, that there are good algorithms which solve similar but a little weaker tasks in the sense that the determined overorder is \(p\)-maximal for a given finite set of primes \(p\). Also, he establishes a relation between the computation of a maximal order and the resolution of plane curve singularities.


All efforts of finding algorithms for unit and class group computations which are at least subexponential depend on the generalized Riemann hypothesis for number fields and --- so far --- other reasonable but unproved assumptions (except for quadratic fields). One of the major ingredients of those algorithms is usually an estimate for the product of the regulator \(R\) and the class number \(h\) of the number field \(F\). The author presents some nice upper bounds for \(h\) as well as for \(hR\).


Besides several new results the paper gives an excellent survey on existing algorithms from a viewpoint of complexity rather than practical performance. It contains numerous references on the latest developments of the theory.

Wilson}, Discrete Appl. Math. 22, 149-161 (1989; Zbl 0661.12007)]; in the case of equality, the normal basis is called optimal. In the paper, all optimal normal bases are determined. editorial_contributions.text:
The facts that (i) every finite field has cardinality \(p^ n\) for some prime number p and some positive integer n, (ii) if p is a prime number and n a positive integer then there exists a field of cardinality \(p^ n\), and (iii) any two fields of cardinality \(p^ n\) are isomorphic, were established by E. H. Moore in 1893. This paper gives an algorithmic version of these results. If \(e_ 1,e_ 2,...,e_ n\) denotes the standard basis of \(F^ p_ n\) over \(F_ p\) then by explicit data for a finite field is meant a system of \(n^ 3\) elements \((a_{ijk})^ n_{i,j,k=1}\) such that \(e_ ie_ j=\sum^{n}_{k=1}a_{ijk}e_ k.\) The following two main theorems are established: 


Theorem 1: There exists a polynomial-time algorithm that, given a prime number p, a positive integer n, and any of (a), (b), and (c), constructs the two others: (a) Explicit data for a field of cardinality \(p^ n\); (b) an irreducible polynomial in \(F_ p[X]\) of degree n; (c) for each prime number r dividing n, an irreducible polynomial in \(F_ p[X]\) of degree r. 


Theorem 2: There exists a polynomial-time algorithm that, given explicit data for two finite fields of the same cardinality, finds an isomorphism between them.

editorial_contributions.text:
The paper provides a deterministic algorithm which decides the primality of a natural number \(n\)\, with complexity \((\log n)^6(2+\log\log n)^c\)\, bits, \(c\)\, a real number effectively computable. This improves a previous result due to \textit{M. Agrawal} et al. [Ann. Math. (2) 160, No. 2, 781--793 (2004; Zbl 1071.11070)] with complexity that look similar, but with exponent \(21/2\)\, instead of \(6\). Both papers follow similar ideas using a mixture of algebraic and  analytic number theory tools.

The proof needs a result from additive number theory due to \textit{D. Bleichenbacher} [The continuous postage problem. Unpublished manuscript (2003)], (see Theorems 3 and 4 of the present paper) and it reasons in some ring extensions of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\)\, (pseudofields,  finite fields if \(n\)\, is a prime), extensions constructed following and improving the construction of finite fields of \textit{L. M. Adleman} and \textit{H. W. Lenstra jun.} [``Finding irreducible polynomials over finite fields'', in: Proceedings of the eighteenth annual ACM symposium on theory of computing, STOC 1986. New York, NY: Association for Computing Machinery (ACM), 350--355 (1986; \url{doi:10.1145/12130.12166})], which adds to  \(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}\)\, a set of \textit{Gaussian periods} parametrized by a \textit{period system}.

 Section 1 enunciates the main  result (Theorem 1) and the auxiliary results necessaries to prove it (Theorems 2 to 5) and Section 2 gives the definition of pseudofield and period system and states some properties of them whose proof is delayed to later. Then Section 3 gives the proof of Theorem 1 (see Algorithm 3.3) assuming the validity of the auxiliary results.

The rest of the paper deals with the auxiliary results. Section 4 provides the proof of Theorem 2 (which gives a method to construct finite fields) and Sections 5 to 8  the proof of the properties  of pseudofields states in Section 2.

The following Sections are more analytic. Section 9 gives the proof of Theorem 3 (inspired by the result of Bleichenbacher) and Section 10 a stronger version of Theorem 4 (a number-theoretic application  of Theorem 3). Sections 11 and 12 are devoted to the proof of Theorem 5 and finally Section 13 proves the existence of periodic systems.

editorial_contributions.text:
A motivation to the paper is the following question of \textit{F. Cucker, P. Koiran} and \textit{S. Smale} [J. Symb. Comput. 27, 21-29 (1999; Zbl 0920.11085)]: can one find all rational zeros of a sparse integer polynomial \(\sum _{i} a_i x^i\) (that given by the list of pairs \((i, a_i)\) with \(a_i\neq 0\)) in polynomial time ? The author shows that this is indeed the case. More generally, there is a deterministic algorithm such that for a sparse polynomial \(f\) with coefficients in a number field \(K\), and a positive integer \(d\), the algorithm finds all monic irreducible factors of \(f\) (in \(K[x]\)) of degree at most \(d\), and their multiplicities, in time at most \((l+d)^c\), where \(l\) denotes the ``length'' of the input data, and \(c\) is a positive absolute and effectively computable constant. The precise definition of the length of the input data is given in his earlier paper [Bull. Am. Math. Soc. 26, 211-244 (1992; Zbl 0759.11046)], and it is essentially the number of bits needed to spell out the data in binary. 


There are also several auxiliary algorithms, one of which finds the cyclotomic factors of \(f\). The key proposition uses the uniform lower bound on the Mahler measure, \(\log M(\alpha)\geq 2\big(\log (3d)\big)^{-3}\), where \(\alpha\) is a non-cyclotomic algebraic number of degree at most \(d\), \(d \geq 2\).

For the entire collection see [Zbl 0911.00025].

editorial_contributions.text:
Suppose \(L\) is a finite extension of the field of \(p\)-adic numbers, and \(k\) is a positive integer. The author proves an upper bound for the positive integer \(B=B(k,L)\) with the following property: if \(f\), \(f\neq 0\), is a polynomial with coefficients in \(L\), and has at most \(k+1\) non-zero terms, then \(f\) has at most \(B\) nonvanishing zeros in \(L\) counted with multiplicities. For trinomials, \(f=a+bx^t+cx^u\), where \(a, b, c\) are \(2\)-adic numbers, the bound \(B\leq 6\) is shown to be sharp. 


As a consequence, the author obtains an upper bound for the degree \(A=A(m,k,d)\) of \(g\), a divisor of \(f\), such that every irreducible factor is of degree at most \(d\). Here, \(f\) is a non-zero polynomial with coefficients in a number field of degree less than or equal to \(m\), and with at most \(k+1\) non-zero terms. In particular, by Descartes' rule of signs, one can take \(A(1,k,1)=2k\). The proofs are based on certain non-archimedean estimates. The author asks for the best values of the involved constants.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 0911.00025].

editorial_contributions.text:
[For the entire collection see Zbl 0657.00005.] 


The problem under consideration is the prime factor decomposition problem and the use of elliptic curve to find solutions to it. One considers two stages: firstly one decides whether a given large integer is a prime or not; secondly, if it is composite, one searches for a nontrivial divisor. 


Applications are found in cryptography. This is based on the fact that primality testing is relatively easy, whereas factorization is hard. After surveying the older algorithms, the author explains the necessary tools from elliptic curve theory, especially point counting theorems and algorithms. He then applies the theory to primality testing on the one hand and to factorization on the other, providing solutions that lead (e.g. method of Atkins) to algorithms that can be used in practical implementations. 


Together with the algorithms, the author discusses running time or probable running time. Not only primality test are discussed. Summary: This paper is devoted to the description and analysis of a new algorithm to factor positive integers. It depends on the use of elliptic curves. The new method is obtained from \textit{J. M. Pollard}'s \(p-1\)-method [Proc. Camb. Philos. Soc. 76, 521--528 (1974; Zbl 0294.10005)] by replacing the multiplicative group by the group of points on a random elliptic curve. It is conjectured that the algorithm determines a non-trivial divisor of a composite number \(n\) in expected time at most \(K(p)(\log n)^2\), where \(p\) is the least prime dividing \(n\) and \(K\) is a function for which 
\[
 \log K(x)=\sqrt{(2+o(1))\log x \log \log x}\quad\text{for } x\to \infty. 
\]
 In the worst case, when \(n\) is the product of two primes of the same order of magnitude, this is 
\[
 \exp ((1+o(1))\sqrt{\log n\log\log n}\quad (\text{for } n\to \infty). 
\]
 There are several other factoring algorithms of which the conjectural expected running time is given by the latter formula. However, these algorithms have a running time that is basically independent of the size of the prime factors of \(n\), whereas the new elliptic curve method is substantially faster for small \(p\).

The authors main result is the following theorem: If the length of the \({\mathfrak O}\)-module \((\text{ker } \pi\phi)/(\text{ker } \pi\phi)^2\) is finite and less than or equal to the length of \({\mathfrak O}/\pi(\text{Ann}_B \text{ ker } \pi)\), then \(B\) is a complete intersection, \(\pi(\text{Ann}_B \text{ ker } \pi)\neq 0\), and \(\pi\) is an isomorphism. (Actually the converse is also true.) As the author points out, the theorem is a generalization of a result due to Wiles in the case in which \(B\) is a Gorenstein ring. The reviewer's impression is that the topic treated in the paper is closely related to an investigation by \textit{G. Scheja} and \textit{U. Storch} [J. Reine Angew. Math. 278/279, 174-190 (1975; Zbl 0316.13003) and Manuscr. Math. 19, 75-104 (1976; Zbl 0329.13011)]. Suppose that the \(B\)-module \(\Omega_{B/{\mathfrak O}}\) of Kähler differentials has finite length. Then \(B\) is a complete intersection if and only if \(\mu(\text{Ann}_{B^e} (\text{Ker }\mu))\) is a principal ideal and equal to the Kähler different \(F_B(\Omega_{B/{\mathfrak O}})\).

Let \(\alpha>0\) be a real number, \(r\) and \(s\) be two coprime integers, and \(n\) an integer such that \(s>n^{\alpha}\). The author proves the following results:

Does \(c(\alpha)\) exist for \(\alpha\leq 1/4?\)

editorial_contributions.text: The author presents the following simplification of G. L. Miller's primality criterion [J. Comput. Syst. Sci. 13, 300--317 (1976; Zbl 0349.68025)]. Assume that for every integer \(d\equiv 1\pmod 4\), which is either prime or the product of two primes, the \(L\)-function \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty (k\mid d) k^{-s}\) satisfies the generalized Riemann hypothesis, where \((k\mid d)\) is the Jacobi symbol. The author shows that the Jacobi symbol \((a/b)\) may be evaluated over \(A\) a ring of algebraic integers in logarithmic efficiency, where \(a\) is an integer and \(b\) is an ideal. (Over \(\mathbb{Z}\), of course, there are well-known reciprocity laws and the Euclidean algorithm, which are lacking in general rings \(A\).)

editorial_contributions.text:
[For the entire collection see Zbl 0596.00003.] 


Several years ago, Goppa and Tsfasman used curves over finite fields to produce a new class of algebraic codes, with particularly striking asymptotic properties [see \textit{M. A. Tsfasman}, \textit{S. G. Vlădut} and \textit{Th. Zink}, Math. Nachr. 109, 21-28 (1982; Zbl 0574.94013)]. In particular, these codes beat the Gilbert-Varshamov bound. In the present paper the well-known analogy between algebraic number fields and curves over a finite field is exploited to construct a similar class of codes with the help of algebraic number fields. The use of the Riemann-Roch theorem is then replaced by considerations from the geometry of numbers. The presence of archimedean valuations poses some problems. First, it causes the new codes to be non-linear. Secondly, it leads to a non- constructive element in the description of the codes so that the question of finding encoding and decoding algorithms - already difficult for the codes of Goppa and Tsfasman - cannot yet be addressed. 


The asymptotic properties of this new class of codes are also investigated. The results obtained are rather weak: the codes obtained cannot be better than Plotkin's upper bound, which is obvious, but they are at least as good, roughly speaking, as the codes that the Gilbert- Varshamov bound predicts to exist. Better results are obtained if the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis is assumed, which is, after all, available in the case of algebraic curves over a finite field. With this assumption, the new codes cannot be as good asymptotically as those of Goppa and Tsfasman, but they are better than the Gilbert-Varshamov codes. The proof of the first statement depends on Weil's explicit formulae in the theory of prime numbers, and the proof of the second statement on the construction of a special infinite class field tower. How good exactly the new codes are is an open problem, even when the truth of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis is assumed.

Let \(L/K\) be a Galois extension of fields with (profinite) Galois group \(G\), and let \((G,K)\) denote the \(K\)-vector space of all continuous functions \(G\to K\), where \(G\) (resp. \(K\)) is endowed with the Krull (resp. the discrete) topology. The group \(G\) acts on \((G,K)\) by left translations. 


Theorem 1. There exists an isomorphism \((G,K)\to L\) of \(K\)-vector spaces that respects the action of \(G\). 


Next, let U denote the set of open normal subgroups of \(G\). If \(N,N'\in U\) and \(N\subset N'\), the group homomorphism \(G/N\to G/N'\) induces a homomorphism \(K[G/N]\to K[G/N']\) of the group rings. Let \(K[[G]]=\lim_{N{\overset \leftarrow  \in}U}K[G/N]\), the limit being taken with respect to these homomorphisms. For each \(N\in U\) the fixed field \(L^ N\) of N is a finite Galois extension of \(K\) with group \(G/N\). If \(N\subset N'\) we have a trace map \(Tr_{N'/N}: L^ N\to L^{N'}\), defined by \(Tr_{N'/N}(y)=\sum_{\sigma \in N'/N}\sigma(y)\). The inverse limit \(\lim_{N{\overset \leftarrow  \in}U}L^ N\) relative to these homomorphisms is naturally a \(K[[G]]\)-module. 


Theorem 2. \(\lim_{N{\overset \leftarrow  \in}U}L^ N\) is a free \(K[[G]]\)-module of rank one. 


When \(L/K\) is finite Galois, both theorems reduce to the normal basis theorem.

R sei ein Dedekindscher Integritätsbereich und P die Menge seiner Primideale. Es ist bekannt, daß jedes Ideal von R ein Hauptideal ist, wenn P endlich ist. \textit{L. Claborn} [Proc. Am. Math. Soc. 18, 378-380 (1967; Zbl 0145.275)] hat bewiesen, daß das gleiche gilt, falls \(| R| >| P|^{\aleph_ 0}\) ist. Wenn P endlich ist, hat \textit{P. Samuel} [J. Algebra 19, 282-301 (1971; Zbl 0223.13019)] gezeigt, daß R sogar euklidisch ist. Dies bedeutet, daß eine Abbildung f von \(R\setminus 0\) in eine wohlgeordnete Menge W existiert mit der Eigenschaft, daß es für je zwei Elemente \(a\quad und\quad b\quad in\quad R\), \(b\neq 0\), \(a\not\in Rb\), ein \(r\in a+Rb\) gibt mit \(f(r)<f(a).\) 


Verf. beweist eine Verschärfung des Clabornschen Satzes, die insbesondere folgenden Satz nach sich zieht: Ein Dedekindscher Integritätsbereich R wie oben ist sogar euklidisch, falls \(| R| >| P|^{\aleph_ 0}\) gilt; als W kann \(\omega^ 2\) benutzt werden, wobei \(\omega\) die Ordnungszahl der natürlichen Zahlen bezeichnet.

The authors sketch the life of N. G. Chebotarëv (1894-1947), most famous for his density theorem in algebraic number theory. Two-thirds of the paper are devoted to Chebotarëv's mathematics. These include a brief history and explanation of the density theorem and its importance, together with a sketch of a proof of it which does not use class field theory (the historical situation). Also included are two further results of Chebotarëv; one on Vandermonde determinants, which has application to the singularities of gap series, and one dealing with whether a certain class of numbers is constructible.


The paper, both mathematically and historically, is very clearly written. There is a picture of Chebotarëv. One small note: while transliteration is always a problem, and the Mathematical Review Journals' standard is an appropriate one to follow, it is nevertheless a little strange to see Alexander Ostrowski (who, though Russian, spent his career in German speaking institutions, chiefly Göttingen and Basel) referred to as Ostrovskii.

editorial_contributions.text:
In a previous paper, the first and third author [Proc. Lond. Math. Soc. (3), 121, 4, 927--953, (2020; Zbl 1470.11275)] showed how to construct counterexamples to the Cohen-Lenstra-Martinet heuristics on class groups of number fields. The present paper continues this study and constructs new infinite series of counterexamples, this time using non-abelian groups. The authors then propose a modified heuristic that uses Arakelov class groups. The Pontryagin dual \(\text{Ar}_F\) of the Arakelov class group of a number field \(F\) sits in an exact sequence 
\[
0\to \text{Hom}(\text{Cl}_F, \mathbb Q/\mathbb Z) \to \text{Ar}_F\to \text{Hom}(\mathcal{O}_F^{\times}, \mathbb Z)\to 0,
\]
where \(\text{Cl}_F\) is the ideal class group, so \(\text{Ar}_F\) takes into account both the ideal class group and the group of units.

Fix a number field \(K\). Let \(G\) be a finite group and let \(\Lambda\) be the quotient of \(\mathbb Z[\frac1{2\#G}][G]\) by the two-sided ideal generated by \(\sum_{g\in G} g\). It is proved that when \(F/K\) is a Galois extension with group \(G\), there are restrictions on where \(\Lambda\otimes \text{Cl}_F\) lives in the Grothendieck group of \(\Lambda\) and it is shown how a conjecture known as Chinburg's \(\Omega(3)\) conjecture also places restrictions. This yields counterexamples to the Cohen-Lenstra-Martinet heuristics in cases where Chinburg's \(\Omega(3)\) conjecture is known to hold. Also, it is proposed that the heuristics should be modified by restricting to only those \(\Lambda\)-modules that satisfy Chinburg's conjecture.

editorial_contributions.text: A number of tests for the primality of a given number \(n\) are shown to follow a pattern, which can be summarized as follows. Let \(G\) be a group such that the set of divisors of \(n\) is mapped to \(G\) by \(\sigma\) in such a way that \(\sigma(rr')=\sigma(r)\sigma(r')\) if \(rr'\) divides \(n\). This can be done by taking \(G\) as the Galois group of a finite abelian field \(K\) such that \((\Delta_K,n)=1\); let \(K\subset\mathbb Q(\zeta_n)\) for some integer \(s\) with \((s,n)=1\) and let \(\sigma\) be the automorphism of \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_s)\) that sends \(\zeta_s\) to \(\zeta^r_s\). It has now been shown that \(\sigma(r)\) is a power of \(\sigma(n)\) for every \(r\) dividing \(n\). This can be done by letting \(A\) be the ring of integers of the field defined by \(\sigma(n)x=x\) and finding a ring homomorphism \(A\to\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z\) (one-to-one). It is proved that this can be done if \(n\) is prime. The information obtained enables limitations to be put on the possible factors of \(n\), and so to show that there are none other than 1 and \(n\). The Lucas-Lehmer test for the primality of \(n=2^n-1\) is analysed in detail: here \(s\) is taken to be \(2^{n+1}\) and the ring is the residue ring of polynomials modulo \(T^2-\sqrt{2} T-1\). (Note that \(\sqrt{2}\equiv 2^{(n+1)/2}\pmod n\in\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z\).)

editorial_contributions.text: Let G be a group and H a subgroup. It is shown that the set of indices \(\{\) [H: \(H\cap gHg^{-1}]|\) \(g\in G\}\) has a finite upper bound n if and only if there is a normal subgroup \(N\trianglelefteq G\) which is commensurable with H; i.e., such that [H:N\(\cap H]\) and [N:N\(\cap H]\) are finite; moreover, the latter indices admit bounds depending only on n. If the bounded index hypothesis is assumed only for g running over some subgroup \(K\leq G\), the conclusion holds with ``normal'' weakened to ``normalized by K''. More detailed information is gotten under the assumption that \(\{[H:H\cap gHg^{-1}]|\) \(g\in G\}=\{1,p\}\) for p prime. In particular, when \(p=2\) there exists \(N\trianglelefteq G\) such that either H has index 2 in N, or N has index 2 in H.

editorial_contributions.text:
This paper provides efficient deterministic algorithms relative to the idempotents and the roots of the unit in an order \(A\)\, (a commutative ring with additive group isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}^n\)). In particular, the paper gives an algorithm with polynomial complexity which computes the set of the primitive idempotents of \(A\) (Theorem 1.1 and Algorithm 6.1) and a polynomial algorithm finding generators and relations for the group \(\mu(A)\)\, of the roots of unity of \(A\) (Theorem 1.2 and Algorithm 13.2). The paper also proves that the discrete logarithm on \(\mu(A)\)\, can be solved in polynomial time (Theorem 1.3). Therefore this group is not suitable for cryptographic purposes.

Section 1 gives an summary of the proof of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2. ``It makes use of several techniques from commutative algebra that so far have found little employment in an algorithmic context.''

Algorithm 6.1 is given in Section 6 and Section 7 provides the proof of Theorem 1.3. The rest of the paper deals with the tools and the intermediate necessary steps and algorithms underlying Theorem 1.1. Algorithm 13.1 is given in Section 13.

editorial_contributions.text:
The paper provides an algorithm that, given an integer \(n\), finds the largest integer \(k\) such that \(n\) is a \(kth\) power. The algorithm has run-time \(\log(n)(\log\log(n))^{O(1)}\), improving a previous algorithm by the first author [Math. Comput. 67, 1253--1283 (1998; Zbl 0910.11057)], taking time \(\log(n)^{1+o(1)}\).

The paper begins listing the three steps of the proposed algorithm: roughly the first step takes for each prime power \(q\) an approximation \(r_q\) to \(n^{1/q}\) while the second finds a 
factor base \(P\) of coprime integers such that \(n\) and each \(r_q\) are a product of powers of elements of \(P\). Finally step 3 finds \(k\) as a gcd.

Then the paper discuss details of the three steps, showing standard ways to perform each step in the mentioned time. Next the authors discuss the performance of the algorithm and they compare it with the previous algorithm of D. J. Bernstein. They point out that for almost all values of \(n\) the first step of the algorithm already reveals that \(k=1\).

Finally the authors review the history of the problem.

editorial_contributions.text:
Let K be a field with a discrete valuation v with perfect residue field k. Let further A be an abelian variety of dimension g over K having purely additive reduction at v; this condition means that the connected component of the special fibre \(A_ 0\) of the Néron minimal model of A at v is a unipotent linear group over k. - For a prime number \(\ell\), let \(\ell^{b(\ell)}\) be the order of the \(\ell\)-primary part of A(K), with \(b(\ell)=\{0,1,2,...,\infty \}.\) The main theorem of this paper asserts that, with these hypotheses and notations, we have \(\sum (\ell - 1)b(\ell)\leq 2g,\) where the sum ranges over all prime numbers \(\ell \neq char(k)\). In particular A(K) has no \(\ell\)-torsion if \(\ell >2g+1.\) 


The proof depends on monodromy arguments. Examples show that the inequality is best possible and that the restriction \(\ell \neq char(k)\) is essential. - It is a consequence of the main theorem that the number m of geometric components of \(A_ 0\) satisfies \(\sum (\ell - 1)ord_{\ell}(m)\leq 2g,\) where the sum is over the same \(\ell\). This improves a result of \textit{J. H. Silverman} [Math. Ann. 264, 1-3 (1983; Zbl 0497.14016)]. It is not clear whether \(\ell =char(k)\) can be included in this sum. The paper concludes with some examples regarding the behaviour of points of order char(k) under the reduction map \(A(K)\to A_ 0(k).\)

editorial_contributions.text:
This paper describes a version of the Adleman, Pomerance, and Rumely (APR) primality algorithm. [\textit{L. M. Adleman}, \textit{C. Pomerance} and \textit{R. S. Rumely}, Ann. Math. (2)117, 173--206 (1983; Zbl 0526.10004)]. The new algorithm is both theoretically and computationally simpler than the APR technique. The development of this idea requires a number of results not usually associated with the problem of primality testing. For example, techniques from the theory of cyclotomic fields are used to reformulate the APR test in terms of Jacobi sums. This reformulation results in congruences, involving these sums, which are much easier to test than those needed by the APR algorithm. The exposition of these developments is pretty-well self-contained and the algorithm is discussed in considerable detail. 

The resulting primality test is very efficient in practice. To give some indication of just how powerful this test is, a PASCAL program implementing the test on CDC Cyber 170-750 computer can routinely handle 100 digit numbers within 45 seconds. Also, a FORTRAN version of this test, implemented on the same machine, can dispose of numbers of up to 200 digits in about 10 minutes or less. These remarkable speeds are much greater than those of any previously developed primality test.

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(D\) be a rational non-square integer and let \(h(D)\) be the class number of the quadratic field \({\mathbb Q}(\sqrt{D})\). The authors give a quantitative heuristic explanation of several observed phenomena concerning the class groups of both real and imaginary quadratic fields. For example, they are able to predict that if \(D<0\), then \(p\mid h(D)\) with approximate probability 43.987\% when \(p=3\) and 23.967\% when \(p=5\). Further, the proportion of real quadratic fields with class number 1 is approximately 75.446\%. Some discussion is also devoted to extending the ideas developed here to fields of higher degree, for example cyclic cubic fields. 

A more detailed version of the paper, including proofs, is to be published elsewhere [Number theory, Proc. Journ. arith., Noodwijkerhout/Neth. 1983, Lect. Notes Math. 1068, 33--62 (1984; Zbl 0558.12002)].

editorial_contributions.text: A normal basis \((\alpha,\alpha^ q,\alpha^{q^ 2},...,\alpha^{q^{m-1}})\) of \({\mathbb{F}}_{q^ m}\) over \({\mathbb{F}}_ q\) is called a primitive normal basis if \(\alpha\) is a primitive element of \({\mathbb{F}}_{q^ m}\). Carlitz proved in 1952 that for all sufficiently large \(q^ m\) there is such a primitive normal basis. Davenport proved in 1968 that a primitive normal basis exists for all m if q is prime. In this paper that result is extended for all prime powers \(q>1\).
